hook_text: Nobody sets the rand's price. Two queues do — and you can learn to read them.
clip_script: Everything on the shelf has a price in rands. Here's the loop nobody explains at school: the rand ITSELF has a price — call it nineteen to the dollar — and it moves exactly the way tomato prices move. Buyers and sellers. Picture two queues at a counter. Queue one BUYS dollars with rands: the fuel importer, the electronics chain restocking phones, parents paying a son's fees at a foreign university, a pension fund buying American shares. Queue two SELLS dollars for rands: the coal exporter paid by India, citrus farmers paid by Europe, tourists changing money at the airport, foreign funds buying our government bonds. Long buying queue, short selling queue? The dollar gets dearer — the rand WEAKENS. Swap the queues and the rand FIRMS. Now read the headlines. Drought forces wheat imports: buy queue swells — rand weakens. Ratings downgrade makes foreign funds dump our bonds: sell queue empties — rand drops hard. Record citrus harvest lands in European supermarkets: export dollars pour in — rand firms. Interest rates rise and our bonds look juicy: money queues to come in — rand firms. Four headlines, one picture. And who controls the price? Nobody. The rand floats, and the queues decide. Bumpy — but honest.
visual_style: A bank counter with two snaking queues of tiny characters — a tanker truck, a phone carton, an orange crate, a tourist with a suitcase — swelling and shrinking while a big R-per-dollar board ticks above them.
pacing: Quick introductions of each queue member, then rapid-fire headline tests, landing on a steady closing line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain any rand headline — plus the balance of payments behind it — in two sentences.
